Changes from the pre-registration

← Back to Online Supplement

Here, we describe all changes from the pre-registration to the manuscript. Note that the pre-registration is available as a PDF in the “files” section of the OSF registration.

It is worth noting some changes to the numbering of research questions from the pre-registration to the manuscript. Pre-registration research question 3 has been moved to the descriptive statistics section. Pre-registration questions 4 and 5 have been merged into manuscript research question 3.

All Research Questions

Major Changes

  • Participation time points 2, 7, and 14 were dropped from all analyses because not all participants were eligible to participate at these time points.
  • To shorten the manuscript and reduce the number of analyses, for research questions 4–5 we focused only on the four adolescence measures and did not analyse the toddlerhood measures.
  • The pre-registration did not specify exclusion criteria; we therefore applied the standard TEDS exclusion criteria provided in the online documentation.

RQ1

Major Changes

  • Instead of fitting multivariate logistic regression models, we used univariate (single outcome) logistic regression with cluster-robust standard errors and Wald tests.
  • McFadden’s R^2 was added as a measure of prediction accuracy.
  • Participation in web tests and questionnaires at the same time point was modelled separately.

Minor Changes

  • We dropped the following variables from the analyses: twin genetic problems (agenpro1/2), mother/father social class (amoclass/afaclass), mother/father has a job (amojob/afajob), mother/father needs special qualification for job (amospq/afaspq).

RQ2

Major Changes

  • We added baseline maternal education as an outcome variable.
  • We dropped anxiety symptoms (GAD-D) as an outcome variable.
  • As with RQ1, we omitted Hellinger’s distance and SRMR from the models, and compared variances and correlations instead of covariances.
  • Outcomes were narrowed to single time points. Where the pre-registration specified each phenotype across multiple ages (e.g., depression at ages 12, 16, 21, and 26), the manuscript analyses each outcome at a single age (Cognitive Y12, GCSE Y16, Depression Y12, Externalising Y12).
  • Twin models were fitted separately by sex.

RQ3

Major Changes

  • Instead of generating time-point-specific weights, we created individualised weights for each variable and pair of variables, as several variables showed uneven missingness even within the same time point.
  • IP-weight truncation at the 1st and 99th percentiles was added (not pre-specified).
  • We increased the number of imputations from 100 to 250.

Minor Changes

  • Instead of using IP weights fitted to model participation at a given timepoint, we used IP weights fitted to model missingness in each variable or pair of variables.
  • We increased the number of imputed datasets to 250 and iterations to 75.

Descriptive Statistics

Descriptive Statistics: All Study Variables

The table below lists every variable used across the analyses, grouped into four panels: (A) baseline variables used to predict later participation and for IP weighting, (B) participation indicators at each wave (1 = participated, 0 = did not), (C) toddlerhood outcome measures (RQ2), and (D) adolescent outcome measures (RQ2-3). For each variable we report a short label, a description, the TEDS variable code (an asterisk denotes a code that was recoded/renamed from the raw TEDS data), the observed range or factor levels, the mean and variance, the number of non-missing observations, and the study wave at which it was collected.

Code
# Function to map variable prefix to study wave
get_study_wave = function(var_name) {
  prefix = substr(var_name, 1, 1)
  wave_map = c(
    "a" = "1st Contact",
    "b" = "2 Year",
    "c" = "3 Year",
    "d" = "4 Year",
    "e" = "In Home",
    "g" = "7 Year",
    "h" = "8 Year",
    "i" = "9 Year",
    "j" = "10 Year",
    "l" = "12 Year",
    "n" = "14 Year",
    "p" = "16 Year",
    "r" = "18 Year",
    "u" = "21 Year",
    "z" = "26 Year"
  )
  return(wave_map[prefix])
}

# Function to clean description labels
clean_description = function(x) {
  x %>%
    # Remove range info at end (e.g., ", 0-22", ", 1-9", ", 4-11")
    str_remove(", \\d+-\\d+$") %>%
    # Remove "see value labels"
    str_remove(", see value labels") %>%
    str_remove("see value labels") %>%
    # Spell out abbreviations inline
    str_replace("SOC employment", "Standard Occupational Classification employment") %>%
    str_replace("MHQ\\)", "Mental Health Questionnaire)") %>%
    str_replace("SLQ\\)", "questionnaire)") %>%
    str_replace("G-game", "G-game (general cognitive ability)") %>%
    str_replace_all(" qnr", " questionnaire") %>%
    # Clean up extra whitespace

    str_squish()
}

# Nominal (unordered) factors: no meaningful mean, excluded from Mean/Variance columns
nominal_vars = c("afasoc2", "amosoc2", "aethnicc", "alang")

# Factors whose level order does not follow the intended ordinal scale (mother/father
# qualification codes come from different underlying SPSS numeric codes), so we map
# them onto a common, substantively-ordered scale instead of using the raw level order
quals_vars = c("afahqual", "amohqual")
quals_order = c(
  "no qualifications",
  "CSE grade 2-5 or O-level/GCSE grade D-G",
  "CSE grade 1 or O-level/GCSE grade A-C",
  "A-level or S-level",
  "HNC",
  "HND",
  "undergraduate degree",
  "postgraduate qualification"
)

# Returns a numeric vector suitable for mean()/var(), or NULL for nominal variables.
# Dichotomous/ordinal factors are recoded using their level order (reference/lowest
# level, marked with "*" in the Range/Level column, = 0), matching the existing table convention.
numeric_for_stats = function(var, df, nominal_vars = character(0), quals_vars = character(0), quals_order = NULL) {
  if (var %in% nominal_vars) return(NULL)
  x = df[[var]]
  if (var %in% quals_vars) return(match(as.character(x), quals_order))
  if (is.factor(x)) return(as.numeric(x) - 1)
  if (is.numeric(x)) return(as.numeric(x))
  NULL
}

get_mean_col = function(vars, df, nominal_vars = character(0), quals_vars = character(0), quals_order = NULL) {
  sapply(vars, function(var) {
    x = numeric_for_stats(var, df, nominal_vars, quals_vars, quals_order)
    if (is.null(x)) NA_real_ else mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  })
}

get_var_col = function(vars, df, nominal_vars = character(0), quals_vars = character(0), quals_order = NULL) {
  sapply(vars, function(var) {
    x = numeric_for_stats(var, df, nominal_vars, quals_vars, quals_order)
    if (is.null(x)) NA_real_ else stats::var(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  })
}

v_rq1x =
  data.frame(
    `Short Label` = rq1x_labels_clean,
    Description = rq1x_labels,
    `Teds Code` = ifelse(rq1x %in% colnames(df0), rq1x,paste0(rq1x,"*")),
    `Range or Level` = sapply(rq1x, function(var) {
      if (class(df[[var]]) == "numeric") {
        paste0(round(min(df[[var]], na.rm = TRUE), 2), " — ", round(max(df[[var]], na.rm = TRUE), 2))
      } else if (is.factor(df[[var]])) {
        factor_levels = levels(df[[var]])
        paste(c(paste0(factor_levels[1],"*"), factor_levels[-1]), collapse = ", ")
      } else {
        paste(unique(df[[var]]), collapse = ", ")
      }
    }),
    Mean = get_mean_col(rq1x, df, nominal_vars, quals_vars, quals_order),
    Variance = get_var_col(rq1x, df, nominal_vars, quals_vars, quals_order),
    N = sapply(rq1x, function(var) {
      sum(!is.na(df[[var]]))
    }),
    `Study Wave` = sapply(rq1x, get_study_wave)
  )

v_rq1x$Description = str_remove(v_rq1x$Description,"\\(1st.*")

Participant Ages at Each Timepoint

The table below summarises the age distribution (in years) at each assessment wave, reporting sample size, mean, SD, minimum, 10th/90th percentiles, and maximum.

Code
df_age_long %>%
  mutate(name = factor(name, levels = paste0(var_to_label(colnames(df_age)), " (", colnames(df_age), ")"))) %>%
  group_by(name) %>%
  summarise(
    n = sum(!is.na(value)),
    mean = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    min = min(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    p10 = quantile(value, 0.10, na.rm = TRUE),
    p90 = quantile(value, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE),
    max = max(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  gt() %>%
  cols_label(
    name = "Timepoint",
    n = "N",
    mean = "Mean",
    sd = "SD",
    min = "Min",
    p10 = "10th",
    p90 = "90th",
    max = "Max"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(mean, sd),
    decimals = 2
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(min, p10, p90, max),
    decimals = 1
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = n,
    use_seps = TRUE,
    decimals = 0
  ) %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Participant Age at Each Timepoint"
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  )

Longitudinal patterns of participation in TEDS

For each twin, we computed whether they participated in each of three periods, each comprising multiple waves of data collection: Years 2-10, 12-16, and 18-26. A twin who participated at least once within a period was classified as “observed” for that period; otherwise, they were classified as “missing”.

The plot below shows the number of participants with data at each combination of these periods. For example, 11,825 twins have data across all three periods, and 2,234 have data across Years 2-16 only, but not between 18-26.

The plot clearly shows that attrition is not monotonic: participants who do not take part in one period often re-participate in a later one. For example, 205 twins did not participate between Years 2-16 but returned between Years 18-26, and 936 twins participated only between Years 12-16, not before or after.

Code
df %>%
  select(all_of(pps_times1)) %>%
  mutate_all(~ tidyr::replace_na(., 0) == 1) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(
    `Year 2 - 10 present`  = any(btwdata1, ctwdata1, dtwdata1, gcdata1, icdata1, jcdata1),
    `Year 12 - 16 present` = any(lcwdata1, lcqdata1, pcwebdata1, pcbhdata1, pcl2data1),
    `Year 18 - 26 present` = any(rcqdata1, u1cdata1, zmhdata1, zcdata1)
  ) %>%
  select(ends_with("present")) %>%
  mutate_all(~ na_if(., FALSE)) %>%
  ggmice::plot_pattern(rotate = TRUE) +

Full list of imputation variables (RQ1)

The table below lists every variable included in the single imputation of baseline/predictor data used for RQ1 (see Singly Impute Missing Predictor/Baseline Data), showing the study wave, description, TEDS variable code, observed range or factor levels, number of non-missing observations, and percent missing prior to imputation.

Code
# Function to map variable prefix to study wave
get_study_wave = function(var_name) {
  prefix = substr(var_name, 1, 1)
  wave_map = c(
    "a" = "1st Contact",
    "b" = "2 Year",
    "c" = "3 Year",
    "d" = "4 Year",
    "e" = "In Home",
    "g" = "7 Year",
    "h" = "8 Year",
    "i" = "9 Year",
    "j" = "10 Year",
    "l" = "12 Year",
    "n" = "14 Year",
    "p" = "16 Year",
    "r" = "18 Year",
    "u" = "21 Year",
    "z" = "26 Year"
  )
  if (var_name %in% c("sex1", "zygos")) return("")
  return(wave_map[prefix])
}

rq1_imputation_vars = colnames(df_rq1)
impute_vars_labels = var_to_label(rq1_imputation_vars) %>%
  sapply(., function(x) ifelse(is.null(x[1]), "", x[1]))

# Create formatted table for imputation variables
v_impute = data.frame(
  `Study.Wave` = sapply(rq1_imputation_vars, get_study_wave),
  Description = impute_vars_labels,
  `Teds Code` = ifelse(rq1_imputation_vars %in% colnames(df0), rq1_imputation_vars, paste0(rq1_imputation_vars, "*")),
  `Range or Level` = sapply(rq1_imputation_vars, function(var) {
    if (var %in% colnames(df)) {
      if (class(df[[var]]) == "numeric") {
        paste0(round(min(df[[var]], na.rm = TRUE), 2), " - ", round(max(df[[var]], na.rm = TRUE), 2))
      } else if (is.factor(df[[var]])) {
        factor_levels = levels(df[[var]])
        paste(c(paste0(factor_levels[1], "*"), factor_levels[-1]), collapse = ", ")
      } else {
        paste(unique(df[[var]]), collapse = ", ")
      }
    } else {
      "Variable not found"
    }
  }),
  N = sapply(rq1_imputation_vars, function(var) {
    if (var %in% colnames(df)) {
      sum(!is.na(df[[var]]))
    } else {
      0
    }
  })
) %>% 
  mutate(
    `Percent Missing` = (nrow(df)-N)/nrow(df)
  )

v_impute$Study.Wave[v_impute$Teds.Code=="cohort"]=""

Twin-Level Logistic Regression Coefficients

The table below reports coefficients (with 95% CIs and cluster-robust Wald p-values, clustered by family) from the univariate logistic regressions predicting participation at each study wave from each baseline predictor, one model per outcome column. Cells shaded green indicate a statistically significant predictor (Wald p < .05) for that wave.

Code
# Extract all coefficients from twin models and combine
twinmodels_results0 = do.call(rbind, lapply(1:length(twinmodels), function(i) {
    vcov_robust = clubSandwich::vcovCR(twinmodels[[i]], 
                                    cluster = twinmodels[[i]]$data$famid, 
                                    type = "CR2") 
    coefs       = clubSandwich::conf_int(twinmodels[[i]], vcov = vcov_robust, test = "naive-tp")

    coefs$outcome = rq1y_twin1[i] 
  return(coefs)
}))

Cluster robust Wald tests were used to calculate using the ClubSandwich R package. Note that for dummy variables, Wald tests were performed by constraining all dummy variables in a given set to zero - therefore dummy variables derived from the same categorical variable have the same p-values.

RQ1: Marginal Effects of Maternal Education on Participation

The plot below shows, for each study wave, the model-predicted probability of participation at each level of maternal education (with 95% CIs), holding all other predictors at their observed means/modes. This illustrates how strongly and consistently maternal education predicts later participation across timepoints.

Code
# Calculate average predictions for maternal education variables

# Calculate predictions for all models

all_predictions = map_dfr(1:length(twinmodels), function(i) {
  data_grid = marginaleffects::datagrid(
    model = twinmodels[[i]],
    amohqual = unique
  )

  pred = predict(twinmodels[[i]], newdata = data_grid, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)
  cbind.data.frame(
    data_grid,
    estimate = plogis(pred$fit),
    conf.low  = plogis(pred$fit - 1.96 * pred$se.fit),
    conf.high = plogis(pred$fit + 1.96 * pred$se.fit)
  ) %>%
    mutate(
      outcome = rq1y_twin_labels_clean_extrashort[i],
      amohqual = factor(amohqual, levels = levels(df$amohqual))
    )
})

# Plot all predictions together
all_predictions %>%
  mutate(
    outcome = factor(outcome, levels = rq1y_twin_labels_clean_extrashort)
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = amohqual, y = estimate, group = outcome, color = outcome, shape = outcome)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), width = 0.2) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17, 15, 18, 8, 3, 4, 25, 7)) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.1),
    labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted Participation by Maternal Education Level",
    subtitle = "Predicted probabilities and 95% CIs across all study timepoints",
    x = "Maternal Education Level",
    y = "Predicted Probability of Participation",
    color = "Study Wave",
    shape = "Study Wave",
    caption = "Note: Predictions calculated using logistic regression models fitted separately for each study wave.\nAll other covariates held at their observed means (continuous) or modes (categorical)."
  )

RQ1: Marginal Effects of Ethnicity on Participation

The plot below shows, for each study wave, the model-predicted probability of participation at each level of ethnic origin (with 95% CIs), holding all other predictors at their observed means/modes. This illustrates how strongly and consistently ethnicity predicts later participation across timepoints.

Code
# Calculate average predictions for ethnicity

# Calculate predictions for all models

all_predictions_ethnicity = map_dfr(1:(length(twinmodels)-1), function(i) {
  data_grid = marginaleffects::datagrid(
    model = twinmodels[[i]],
    aethnicc = unique
  )

  pred = predict(twinmodels[[i]], newdata = data_grid, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)
  cbind.data.frame(
    data_grid,
    estimate = plogis(pred$fit),
    conf.low  = plogis(pred$fit - 1.96 * pred$se.fit),
    conf.high = plogis(pred$fit + 1.96 * pred$se.fit)
  ) %>%
    mutate(
      outcome = rq1y_twin_labels_clean_extrashort[i],
      aethnicc = factor(aethnicc, levels = levels(df$aethnicc))
    )
})

# Plot all predictions together
all_predictions_ethnicity %>%
  mutate(
    outcome = factor(outcome, levels = rq1y_twin_labels_clean_extrashort),
    aethnicc = factor(
      aethnicc,
      levels = c("Asian", "White", "Other", "Mixed race", "Black")
    )
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = aethnicc, y = estimate, group = outcome, color = outcome, shape = outcome)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), width = 0.2) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17, 15, 18, 8, 3, 4, 25, 7)) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.1),
    labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted Participation by Ethnic Origin",
    subtitle = "Predicted probabilities and 95% CIs across all study timepoints",
    x = "Ethnicity",
    y = "Predicted Probability of Participation",
    color = "Study Wave",
    shape = "Study Wave",
    caption = "Note: Predictions calculated using logistic regression models fitted separately for each study wave.\nAll other covariates held at their observed means (continuous) or modes (categorical)."
  )

Research Question 2: Effects of Attrition(ing)

Toddlerhood Outcomes - Attritioned vs Original Estimates (Bias)

Toddlerhood Outcomes: Means, SMDs, and Variances

For each toddlerhood outcome, the table below compares the “original” (full) sample to the “attritioned” sample created by setting that outcome to missing for participants who did not take part in a given wave. Row groups correspond to each attritioned wave. Reported for each outcome are the raw mean difference, the standardized mean difference (SMD), and the percentage change in variance (attritioned relative to original), each with bootstrap 95% CIs and Bonferroni-Holm adjusted p-values; statistically significant increases are shaded red and decreases blue.

Code
variable_comparisons_df %>%
  select(-starts_with("."),-pd, -pval) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = "stat",
    values_from = c("y","ymin","ymax","pval_adj"),
    id_cols = c("variable", "dataset")
  ) %>%
  dplyr::rename( Outcome = "variable") %>%
  gt(groupname_col = "dataset") %>%
  tab_options(
    table.width = px(800)
    # table.border.top.style = "none",
    # table.border.bottom.style = "none",
    # column_labels.border.bottom.style = "solid",
    # column_labels.border.bottom.width = px(1),
    # column_labels.border.bottom.color = "black",
    # table_body.border.bottom.style = "none",
    # table_body.vlines.style = "none",
    # row_group.border.bottom.style = "none"
  ) %>%
  
  # Create column spanners (nested headers)
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Mean Difference",
    columns = c(y_md, ymin_md, ymax_md, pval_adj_md)
  ) %>%
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Standardized Mean Difference", 
    columns = c(y_smd, ymin_smd, ymax_smd, pval_adj_smd)
  ) %>%
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Variance % Change",
    columns = c(y_var, ymin_var, ymax_var, pval_adj_var)
  ) %>%
  
  # Rename columns under each spanner
  cols_label(
    y_md = "Est", ymin_md = "LB", ymax_md = "UB", pval_adj_md = "p",
    y_smd = "Est", ymin_smd = "LB", ymax_smd = "UB", pval_adj_smd = "p", 
    y_var = "Est", ymin_var = "LB", ymax_var = "UB", pval_adj_var = "p"
  ) %>%
  
  # Format numbers
  fmt(
    columns = !contains("var") & !contains("Outcome"),
    fns = function(x) {gbtoolbox::apa_num(x, n_decimal_places = 3)}
  ) %>% 
  fmt(
    columns = "pval_adj_var",
    fns = function(x) {gbtoolbox::apa_num(x, n_decimal_places = 3)}
  ) %>% 
  fmt_percent(
    columns = c("y_var", "ymin_var","ymax_var"),
    decimals = 2,
    drop_trailing_zeros = FALSE,
    drop_trailing_dec_mark = FALSE
  ) %>%
  # Styling - uniform font size
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(size = px(10)),
    locations = cells_column_spanners()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(size = px(10)),
    locations = cells_body()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(size = px(10), align = "center"),
    locations = cells_row_groups()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(size = px(10)),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(size = px(10)),
    locations = cells_footnotes()
  ) %>%
  
  # Highlight significant results - positive effects (light red)
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#ffd9d1"),  # Light red for positive effects
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = c(y_md, ymin_md, ymax_md, pval_adj_md),
      rows = pval_adj_md < 0.05 & y_md > 0
    )
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#ffd9d1"),  # Light red for positive effects
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = c(y_smd, ymin_smd, ymax_smd, pval_adj_smd),
      rows = pval_adj_smd < 0.05 & y_smd > 0
    )
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#ffd9d1"),  # Light red for positive effects
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = c(y_var, ymin_var, ymax_var, pval_adj_var),
      rows = pval_adj_var < 0.05 & y_var > 0
    )
  ) %>%

  # Highlight significant results - negative effects (light blue)
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#b6c3e0"),  # Light blue for negative effects
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = c(y_md, ymin_md, ymax_md, pval_adj_md),
      rows = pval_adj_md < 0.05 & y_md < 0
    )
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#b6c3e0"),  # Light blue for negative effects
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = c(y_smd, ymin_smd, ymax_smd, pval_adj_smd),
      rows = pval_adj_smd < 0.05 & y_smd < 0
    )
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#b6c3e0"),  # Light blue for negative effects
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = c(y_var, ymin_var, ymax_var, pval_adj_var),
      rows = pval_adj_var < 0.05 & y_var < 0
    )
  ) %>%

  # Add footnotes
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = md("<em>Note.</em> Est = Estimate, LB = Lower Bound 95% Confidence Interval, UB = Upper Bound 95% Confidence Interval. Significant (p<sub>Bonferroni-Holm</sub>) effects are highlighted in red (increases) or blue (decreases)."),
    # locations = cells_column_spanners(),
    placement = "right"
  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = "P values are Bonferroni-Holm adjusted within each participation group",
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = contains("pval_adj")),
    placement = "right"
  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = md("Standardized mean difference = (Mean<sub>original</sub> - Mean<sub>attritioned</sub>) / SD<sub>original</sub>"),
    locations = cells_column_spanners(spanners = "Standardized Mean Difference"),
    placement = "right"
  ) %>%
    tab_footnote(
    footnote = md("Percentage change = (Var<sub>attritioned</sub> - Var<sub>original</sub>) / Var<sub>original</sub>"),
    locations = cells_column_spanners(spanners = "Variance % Change"),
    placement = "right"
  ) %>%
  opt_footnote_marks(marks = c("*", "†","‡"))

Effect of attrition on the variance of maternal education

Unlike the other outcomes, the variance of maternal education increased after attrition in our main analyses. The tables below show that this depends on how maternal education is coded.

In the original 8-level coding used in our main analyses, the higher qualifications are spread over a wide range of codes (A-levels = 4 to postgraduate = 8), far from the most common category (GCSE grades A–C = 3; see the maternal education distribution). Attrition mainly removed families with lower maternal education, so more of the remaining sample fell into these distant upper categories, increasing variance (e.g., by 10% in the Year 26 web test sample). However, this coding does not appear to reflect equal steps: child outcomes were similar for mothers with A-levels, HNC and HND qualifications (see descriptives). When these three categories are merged into a 6-level coding, variance instead decreased slightly in every attritioned sample (by 1–5%), consistent with the other outcomes.

When maternal education is dichotomised into degree vs. no degree, variance increased after attrition (e.g., by 32% in the Year 26 web test sample). This is expected for a binary variable: its variance, p(1 − p), increases as p moves towards .5, and the proportion of mothers with a degree rose from .18 in the full sample to .26 in the Year 26 web test sample.

Original Coding

Code
entropy = function(x) {
  counts = table(x)
  p = as.numeric(counts) / sum(counts)
  p = p[p > 0]
  -sum(p * log2(p))
}

summary_stats = df %>% 
  mutate(mat_edu = amohqualn1) %>% 
  select(all_of(rq1y_twin1),mat_edu) %>% 
  mutate(fullsample = 1) %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = !mat_edu) %>% 
  group_by(name, value) %>% 
  summarise(
    mean = mean(mat_edu, na.rm = TRUE),
    var  = sd(mat_edu, na.rm = TRUE)^2,
    entropy = entropy(mat_edu),
    n    = dplyr::n()
  ) %>% 
  filter(value == 1)

Combining HNC and HND with A-levels

HNC and HND qualifications are vocational and sit ambiguously between A-levels and undergraduate degrees in the original ordinal coding. Here they are collapsed into the A-level category to create a cleaner 6-level ordinal scale. The table shows the mean, variance, and entropy of the recoded maternal education variable for participants at each study timepoint and for the full sample. Higher entropy indicates a more evenly distributed education profile among participants; a decline in entropy relative to the full sample would indicate that attrition is concentrating the sample toward certain education levels.

Code
# table(df$amohqualn1,  df$amohqual)

df3 = df %>% 
  mutate(
    mat_edu = case_when(
      .default = amohqualn1,
      amohqualn1 == 5 ~ 4,  # HNC -> A level
      amohqualn1 == 6 ~ 4,  # HND -> A level
      amohqualn1 == 7 ~ 5,  # undergraduate degree
      amohqualn1 == 8 ~ 6   # postgraduate qualification

  select(all_of(rq1y_twin1),mat_edu)

Dichotomising education into degree vs. no degree

Here maternal education is reduced to a binary variable: whether or not the mother holds an undergraduate or postgraduate degree. This is a common simplification in the literature and avoids assumptions about the spacing of the ordinal scale. The table shows the proportion of mothers with a degree (mean), variance, and entropy among participants at each timepoint and in the full sample. A rising proportion of degree-educated mothers across timepoints would indicate that attrition disproportionately removes families from lower education backgrounds.

Code
df4 = df %>%
  mutate(
    mat_edu_degree = case_when(
      amohqualn1 >= 7 ~ 1L,  # undergraduate degree or above
      amohqualn1 <  7 ~ 0L,
      .default = NA_integer_
    )
  ) %>%
  select(all_of(rq1y_twin1), mat_edu_degree)

summary_stats_degree = df4 %>%

    var     = sd(mat_edu_degree, na.rm = TRUE)^2,
    entropy = entropy(mat_edu_degree),
    n       = dplyr::n()
  ) %>%
  filter(value == 1)

Toddlerhood Outcomes: Correlations

Below is a results table for the change in correlations. For every pair of toddlerhood outcomes, we compare the correlation in the attritioned sample to the correlation in the original sample (row groups = attrition timepoint), reporting the difference with bootstrap 95% CIs and unadjusted/Bonferroni-Holm adjusted p-values; significant increases are shaded green and decreases red.

Code
cor_table = bind_rows(correlation_comparisons, .id = "timepoint") %>%
  mutate(
    dataset = rq1y_twin_labels_clean_extrashort[match(timepoint, rq1y_twin1)],
    x_var_label = rq2y_labels_short[match(x_var, rq2y)],
    y_var_label = rq2y_labels_short[match(y_var, rq2y)],
    pair = paste(x_var_label, "×", y_var_label)
  ) %>%
  select(dataset, pair, y, ymin, ymax, pval, pval_adj) %>%
  filter(!is.na(dataset)) %>%
  gt(groupname_col = "dataset") %>%
  # tab_options(
  #   table.width = px(800)
  # ) %>%

  # Rename columns
  cols_label(
    pair = "Variable Pair",
    y = "Est",
    ymin = "LB",
    ymax = "UB",
    pval = md("p<sub>unadj</sub>"),
    pval_adj = md("p<sub>adj</sub>")
  ) %>%

  # Create column spanner
  tab_spanner(
    label = md("Correlation difference = Cor<sub>attritioned</sub> - Cor<sub>original</sub>"),
    columns = c(y, ymin, ymax, pval, pval_adj)
  ) %>%

  # Format numbers
  fmt(
    columns = c(y, ymin, ymax),
    fns = function(x) {gbtoolbox::apa_num(x, n_decimal_places = 3)}
  ) %>%
  fmt(
    columns = c(pval, pval_adj),
    fns = function(x) {gbtoolbox::apa_num(x, n_decimal_places = 3)}
  ) %>%

  # Styling - uniform font size
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(size = px(10)),
    locations = cells_column_spanners()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(size = px(10)),
    locations = cells_body()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(size = px(10), align = "center"),
    locations = cells_row_groups()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(size = px(10)),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(size = px(10)),
    locations = cells_footnotes()
  ) %>%

  # Highlight significant results - positive effects (light green)
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#d5e8d4"),
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = c(pair, y, ymin, ymax, pval, pval_adj),
      rows = pval_adj < 0.05 & y > 0
    )
  ) %>%

  # Highlight significant results - negative effects (light red)
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#f8cecc"),
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = c(pair, y, ymin, ymax, pval, pval_adj),
      rows = pval_adj < 0.05 & y < 0
    )
  ) %>%

  # Add footnotes
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = md("<em>Note.</em> Est = Estimate, LB = Lower Bound 95% Confidence Interval, UB = Upper Bound 95% Confidence Interval. Significant (p<sub>Bonferroni-Holm</sub>) effects are highlighted in green (increases) or red (decreases)."),
    placement = "right"
  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = "P values are Bonferroni-Holm adjusted within each attrition timepoint",
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = pval_adj),
    placement = "right"
  ) %>%
  opt_footnote_marks(marks = c("*", "†", "‡"))

Toddlerhood Outcomes: ACE Estimates and Differences

The table below compares the ACE (Additive genetic, shared environment, non-shared environment) variance component estimates from twin models fitted to the original vs. attritioned toddlerhood samples, separately by sex and attrition timepoint. For each outcome and component (A, C, E) it shows the original and attritioned estimates, their difference with bootstrap 95% CI, and a Bonferroni-Holm adjusted p-value (adjusted within each sex/parameter/timepoint group); significant differences are highlighted green.

Code
bootstrap_summary_df_ace %>%
  filter(par %in% c("a","c","e")) %>%
  group_by(dataset_label) %>%
  mutate(
    pval = stats::p.adjust(pval, method = "holm"),
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(-starts_with("."), -n, -pd) %>%
  mutate(name_clean = rq2y_labels_short[match(name, rq2y)]) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = c(par, name_clean, sex, dataset_label),
    names_from = group,
    values_from = c(y, ymin, ymax, pval),
    names_sep = "_"
  ) %>%
  select(-ymin_Original, -ymax_Original, -ymin_Attritioned, -ymax_Attritioned, -pval_Original, -pval_Attritioned) %>%
  select(dataset_label, name_clean, par, y_Original, y_Attritioned, y_Difference, ymin_Difference, ymax_Difference, pval_Difference, sex) %>%
  mutate(
    name_clean    = factor(name_clean,    levels = rq2y_labels_short),
    dataset_label = factor(dataset_label, levels = rq1y_twin_labels_clean_extrashort)
    ) %>% 
  arrange(sex, dataset_label, name_clean, par) %>%
  mutate(par = toupper(par)) %>%
  gt(groupname_col = "sex") %>%
  fmt_number(decimals = 3) %>%
  tab_row_group(
    label = "Male",
    rows = sex == "male"
  ) %>%
  tab_row_group(
    label = "Female",
    rows = sex == "female"
  ) %>%
  cols_hide(sex) %>%
  cols_label(
    dataset_label = "Timepoint",
    name_clean = "Variable",
    par = "",
    y_Original = "Original",
    y_Attritioned = "Attritioned",
    y_Difference = "Diff",
    ymin_Difference = "Lower",
    ymax_Difference = "Upper",
    pval_Difference = "p"
  ) %>%
  tab_spanner(
    label = "95% CI",
    columns = c(ymin_Difference, ymax_Difference)
  ) %>%
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Estimates",
    columns = c(y_Attritioned, y_Original)
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "lightgreen"),
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = everything(),
      rows = pval_Difference < 0.05
    )
  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = "P values are Bonferroni-Holm adjusted within each sex, parameter (A, C or E), and timepoint group",
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = pval_Difference)
  )

Adolescent Outcomes - Attritioned vs Original Estimates (Bias)

Adolescent Outcomes: Means, SMDs, and Variances

For each adolescent outcome, the table below compares the original (full) sample to the attritioned sample created by setting the outcome to missing for participants who did not take part in a given wave, analogous to the toddlerhood comparison. Row groups correspond to each attrition timepoint. Reported for each outcome are the raw mean difference, standardized mean difference (SMD), and percentage change in variance (attritioned relative to original), each with bootstrap 95% CIs and Bonferroni-Holm adjusted p-values; significant increases are shaded green and decreases red.

Code
variable_comparisons_df %>%
  filter(stat %in% c("md", "smd", "var")) %>%
  select(-starts_with("."),-pd) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = "stat",
    values_from = c("y","ymin","ymax","pval","pval_adj"),
    id_cols = c("variable", "dataset")
  ) %>%
  dplyr::rename(Outcome = "variable") %>%
  gt(groupname_col = "dataset") %>%
  tab_options(
    table.width = px(800)
  ) %>%

  # Create column spanners (nested headers)
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Mean Difference",
    columns = c(y_md, ymin_md, ymax_md, pval_md, pval_adj_md)
  ) %>%
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Standardized Mean Difference",
    columns = c(y_smd, ymin_smd, ymax_smd, pval_smd, pval_adj_smd)
  ) %>%
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Variance % Change",
    columns = c(y_var, ymin_var, ymax_var, pval_var, pval_adj_var)
  ) %>%

  # Rename columns under each spanner
  cols_label(
    y_md = "Est", ymin_md = "LB", ymax_md = "UB", pval_md = md("p<sub>unadj</sub>"), pval_adj_md = md("p<sub>adj</sub>"),
    y_smd = "Est", ymin_smd = "LB", ymax_smd = "UB", pval_smd = md("p<sub>unadj</sub>"), pval_adj_smd = md("p<sub>adj</sub>"),
    y_var = "Est", ymin_var = "LB", ymax_var = "UB", pval_var = md("p<sub>unadj</sub>"), pval_adj_var = md("p<sub>adj</sub>")
  ) %>%

  # Format numbers
  fmt(
    columns = !contains("var") & !contains("Outcome"),
    fns = function(x) {gbtoolbox::apa_num(x, n_decimal_places = 3)}
  ) %>%
  fmt(
    columns = c("pval_var", "pval_adj_var"),
    fns = function(x) {gbtoolbox::apa_num(x, n_decimal_places = 3)}
  ) %>%
  fmt_percent(
    columns = c("y_var", "ymin_var","ymax_var"),
    decimals = 2,
    drop_trailing_zeros = FALSE,
    drop_trailing_dec_mark = FALSE
  ) %>%
  # Styling - uniform font size
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(size = px(10)),
    locations = cells_column_spanners()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(size = px(10)),
    locations = cells_body()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(size = px(10), align = "center"),
    locations = cells_row_groups()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(size = px(10)),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(size = px(10)),
    locations = cells_footnotes()
  ) %>%

  # Highlight significant results - positive effects (light green)
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#d5e8d4"),
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = c(y_md, ymin_md, ymax_md, pval_md, pval_adj_md),
      rows = pval_adj_md < 0.05 & y_md > 0
    )
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#d5e8d4"),
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = c(y_smd, ymin_smd, ymax_smd, pval_smd, pval_adj_smd),
      rows = pval_adj_smd < 0.05 & y_smd > 0
    )
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#d5e8d4"),
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = c(y_var, ymin_var, ymax_var, pval_var, pval_adj_var),
      rows = pval_adj_var < 0.05 & y_var > 0
    )
  ) %>%

  # Highlight significant results - negative effects (light red)
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#f8cecc"),
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = c(y_md, ymin_md, ymax_md, pval_md, pval_adj_md),
      rows = pval_adj_md < 0.05 & y_md < 0
    )
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#f8cecc"),
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = c(y_smd, ymin_smd, ymax_smd, pval_smd, pval_adj_smd),
      rows = pval_adj_smd < 0.05 & y_smd < 0
    )
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#f8cecc"),
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = c(y_var, ymin_var, ymax_var, pval_var, pval_adj_var),
      rows = pval_adj_var < 0.05 & y_var < 0
    )
  ) %>%

  # Add footnotes
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = md("<em>Note.</em> Est = Estimate, LB = Lower Bound 95% Confidence Interval, UB = Upper Bound 95% Confidence Interval. Significant (p<sub>Bonferroni-Holm</sub>) effects are highlighted in green (increases) or red (decreases)."),
    placement = "right"
  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = "P values are Bonferroni-Holm adjusted within each participation group",
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = contains("pval_adj")),
    placement = "right"
  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = md("Standardized mean difference = (Mean<sub>original</sub> - Mean<sub>attritioned</sub>) / SD<sub>original</sub>"),
    locations = cells_column_spanners(spanners = "Standardized Mean Difference"),
    placement = "right"
  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = md("Percentage change = (Var<sub>attritioned</sub> - Var<sub>original</sub>) / Var<sub>original</sub>"),
    locations = cells_column_spanners(spanners = "Variance % Change"),
    placement = "right"
  ) %>%
  opt_footnote_marks(marks = c("*", "†","‡"))

Adolescent Outcomes: Correlations

The table below shows, for each pair of adolescent outcomes, the difference between the correlation in the attritioned sample and the correlation in the original sample (row groups = attrition timepoint), with bootstrap 95% CIs and unadjusted/Bonferroni-Holm adjusted p-values; significant increases are shaded green and decreases red.

Code
cor_table = bind_rows(correlation_comparisons, .id = "timepoint") %>%
  mutate(
    dataset = rq1y_twin_labels_clean_extrashort[match(timepoint, rq1y_twin1)],
    x_var_label = rq6y_labels[match(x_var, rq6y)],
    y_var_label = rq6y_labels[match(y_var, rq6y)],
    pair = paste(x_var_label, "×", y_var_label)
  ) %>%
  select(dataset, pair, y, ymin, ymax, pval, pval_adj) %>%
  gt(groupname_col = "dataset") %>%
  tab_options(
    table.width = px(800)
  ) %>%

  # Rename columns
  cols_label(
    pair = "Variable Pair",
    y = "Est",
    ymin = "LB",
    ymax = "UB",
    pval = md("p<sub>unadj</sub>"),
    pval_adj = md("p<sub>adj</sub>")
  ) %>%

  # Create column spanner
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Correlation Difference",
    columns = c(y, ymin, ymax, pval, pval_adj)
  ) %>%

  # Format numbers
  fmt(
    columns = c(y, ymin, ymax),
    fns = function(x) {gbtoolbox::apa_num(x, n_decimal_places = 3)}
  ) %>%
  fmt(
    columns = c(pval, pval_adj),
    fns = function(x) {gbtoolbox::apa_num(x, n_decimal_places = 3)}
  ) %>%

  # Styling - uniform font size
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(size = px(10)),
    locations = cells_column_spanners()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(size = px(10)),
    locations = cells_body()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(size = px(10), align = "center"),
    locations = cells_row_groups()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(size = px(10)),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(size = px(10)),
    locations = cells_footnotes()
  ) %>%

  # Highlight significant results - positive effects (light green)
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#d5e8d4"),
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = c(y, ymin, ymax, pval, pval_adj),
      rows = pval_adj < 0.05 & y > 0
    )
  ) %>%

  # Highlight significant results - negative effects (light red)
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#f8cecc"),
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = c(y, ymin, ymax, pval, pval_adj),
      rows = pval_adj < 0.05 & y < 0
    )
  ) %>%

  # Add footnotes
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = md("<em>Note.</em> Est = Estimate, LB = Lower Bound 95% Confidence Interval, UB = Upper Bound 95% Confidence Interval. Significant (p<sub>Bonferroni-Holm</sub>) effects are highlighted in green (increases) or red (decreases)."),
    placement = "right"
  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = "P values are Bonferroni-Holm adjusted within each attrition timepoint",
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = pval_adj),
    placement = "right"
  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = md("Correlation difference = Cor<sub>attritioned</sub> - Cor<sub>original</sub>"),
    locations = cells_column_spanners(spanners = "Correlation Difference"),
    placement = "right"
  ) %>%
  opt_footnote_marks(marks = c("*", "†", "‡"))

Adolescent Outcomes: Attritioned vs. Original ACE Estimates

The table below compares the ACE (Additive genetic, shared environment, non-shared environment) variance component estimates from twin models fitted to the original vs. attritioned adolescent samples, separately by sex and attrition timepoint. For each outcome and component (A, C, E) it shows the original and attritioned estimates, their difference with bootstrap 95% CI, and a Bonferroni-Holm adjusted p-value (adjusted within each dataset group); significant differences are highlighted green. This mirrors the format of the Toddlerhood Outcomes ACE Estimates and Differences table.

Code
ace_differences_tbl = ace_differences  %>%
  group_by(dataset) %>%
  mutate(
    pval_adj = stats::p.adjust(pval, method = "holm")
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

ace_estimates_wide = ace_estimates %>%
  filter(par %in% c("a", "c", "e")) %>%
  mutate(
    name_clean = rq6y_labels[match(name, rq6y)],
    group = ifelse(group == "df1", "Attritioned", "Original")
  ) %>%
  select(dataset_label, name_clean, par, sex, group, y) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = c(dataset_label, name_clean, par, sex),
    names_from = group,
    values_from = y,
    names_prefix = "y_"
  )

Research Question 3: Evaluating methods for correcting attrition bias

Table of all variables used in multiple imputation (RQ3)

Note that imputation was performed separately across zygosity-sex groups (i.e., MZ males, MZ females, DZ males, …) therefore sex and zygosity are omitted from imputation models.

Because imputations were performed separetely for each attriitoning time point, we calculate FMI for each timepoint and average across.

The table below lists every variable included in the multiple imputation models for RQ3, with its description, TEDS code, observed range/levels, percentage missing in the original sample, mean fraction of missing information (FMI) across timepoints, and study wave.

Code
# Function to map variable prefix to study wave
get_study_wave = function(var_name) {
  if (str_detect(var_name, "^pgs_")) return("Genotyping")                      # polygenic scores
  prefix = substr(var_name, 1, 1)
  wave_map = c(
    "a" = "1st Contact",
    "b" = "2 Year",
    "c" = "3 Year",
    "d" = "4 Year",
    "e" = "In Home",
    "g" = "7 Year",
    "h" = "8 Year",
    "i" = "9 Year",
    "j" = "10 Year",
    "l" = "12 Year",
    "n" = "14 Year",
    "p" = "16 Year",
    "r" = "18 Year",
    "u" = "21 Year",
    "z" = "26 Year"
  )
  return(wave_map[prefix])
}

rq6_imputation_vars = c(rq6y_all, rq6z_vars, rq6z_pgs_vars)
impute_vars_labels = var_to_label(rq6_imputation_vars) %>%
  sapply(., function(x) ifelse(is.null(x[1]), "", x[1]))

# % missing cases in original df
pct_missing = sapply(rq6_imputation_vars, function(var) {
  if (var %in% colnames(df)) {
    round(100 * mean(is.na(df[[var]])), 1)
  } else {
    NA_real_
  }
})

# Fraction of Missing Information (FMI) for sample means across attrition timepoints (numeric vars only)
fmi_by_var = sapply(rq6_imputation_vars, function(v) {
  # Only compute for numeric variables; factors have no meaningful mean FMI
  if (!v %in% colnames(df) || !is.numeric(df[[v]])) return(NA_real_)
  # Calculate FMI for each attritioning timepoint (imputations were run separately for each attritioning timepoint)
  fmi_vals = sapply(seq_along(imputed_mice), function(tp) {
    # browser()
    imp_list = imputed_mice[[tp]]
    if (!v %in% colnames(imp_list[[1]])) return(NA_real_)
    Q = sapply(imp_list, function(d) mean(d[[v]], na.rm = TRUE))
    U = sapply(imp_list, function(d) {
      n_obs = sum(!is.na(d[[v]]))
      if (n_obs < 2) return(NA_real_)
      stats::var(d[[v]], na.rm = TRUE) / n_obs
    })
    tryCatch(
      mice::pool.scalar(Q = Q, U = U)$fmi,
      error = function(e) NA_real_
    )
  })
  mean(fmi_vals, na.rm = TRUE)
})

# Create formatted table for imputation variables
v_impute = data.frame(
  Description = impute_vars_labels,
  `Teds Code` = ifelse(rq6_imputation_vars %in% original_colnames, rq6_imputation_vars, paste0(rq6_imputation_vars, "*")),
  `Range or Level` = sapply(rq6_imputation_vars, function(var) {
    if (var %in% colnames(df)) {
      if (class(df[[var]]) == "numeric") {
        paste0(round(min(df[[var]], na.rm = TRUE), 2), " - ", round(max(df[[var]], na.rm = TRUE), 2))
      } else if (is.factor(df[[var]])) {
        factor_levels = levels(df[[var]])
        paste(c(paste0(factor_levels[1], "*"), factor_levels[-1]), collapse = ", ")
      } else {
        paste(unique(df[[var]]), collapse = ", ")
      }
    } else {
      "Variable not found"
    }
  }),
  N = sapply(rq6_imputation_vars, function(var) {
    if (var %in% colnames(df)) {
      sum(!is.na(df[[var]]))
    } else {
      0
    }
  }),
  `Missing (%)` = pct_missing,
  `FMI (mean)` = round(fmi_by_var, 4),
  `Study.Wave` = sapply(rq6_imputation_vars, get_study_wave),
  check.names = FALSE
)

gt(v_impute) %>%
  cols_label_with(fn = ~ gsub("\\.", " ", .x)) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(size = px(12)),
    locations = cells_body()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(size = px(12)),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) %>%
  cols_hide(N) %>%
  fmt_percent(columns = `FMI (mean)`, decimals = 0) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = `Missing (%)`, decimals = 0, pattern = "{x}%") %>%
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Note: Range or Level shows min-max values for numeric variables or factor levels for categorical variables (reference level marked with *). Variable codes with an asterisk (*) have been derived or modified from the original dataset. Missing (%) is the percentage of missing cases in the original sample. FMI (mean) is the fraction of missing information for the sample mean, averaged across attrition timepoints; NA for factor variables."
  ) %>%
  tab_options(
    table.width = "70%"
  ) %>%
  cols_width(
    Description ~ px(300),
    everything() ~ px(120)
  )

Note: Range or Level shows min-max values for numeric variables or factor levels for categorical variables (reference level marked with *). Variable codes with an asterisk (*) have been derived or modified from the original dataset. Missing (%) is the percentage of missing cases in the original sample. FMI (mean) is the fraction of missing information for the sample mean, averaged across attrition timepoints; NA for factor variables.

Means, Variances & Correlations

RQ3: Attritioned vs. Original (Means, Variances & Correlations)

The table below shows, for each adolescent outcome and attrition timepoint, the standardized mean difference, variance % change, and correlation change between each bias-correction condition (Unadjusted, IP-Weighted, Imputed) and the original full sample, with 95% CIs and Bonferroni-Holm adjusted p-values (adjusted within each condition × timepoint × parameter group). Significant increases relative to the original sample are shaded orange and decreases blue.

Code
bias_summary = combined_results %>%
  group_by(condition, timepoint, stat) %>%
  reframe(
    bias = .mean_qi_pd(value)
  ) %>%
  unnest(bias) %>%
  # Split stat into param and variable(s)
  mutate(
    param = str_extract(stat, "^[^_]+"),
    variable_raw = str_remove(stat, "^[^_]+_")
  ) %>%
  # For correlations, extract both variables
  mutate(
    var1 = case_when(
      param == "cor" ~ str_extract(variable_raw, "^[^_]+"),
      TRUE ~ variable_raw
    ),
    var2 = case_when(
      param == "cor" ~ str_extract(variable_raw, "[^_]+$"),
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) %>%
  # Convert to nice labels
  mutate(
    var1_label = rq6y_labels[match(var1, rq6y)],
    var2_label = rq6y_labels[match(var2, rq6y)],
    variable_label = case_when(
      param == "cor" ~ paste0(var1_label, " × ", var2_label),
      TRUE ~ var1_label
    ),
    param = case_when(
      param == "smd" ~ "Standardized Mean Difference",
      param == "var" ~ "Variance % Change",
      param == "cor" ~ "Correlation Change",
      TRUE ~ param
    ),
    param = factor(param, levels = c("Standardized Mean Difference", "Variance % Change", "Correlation Change"))
  ) %>%
  # Order timepoint, condition, and variables
  mutate(
    timepoint = factor(timepoint, levels = rq1y_twin_labels_clean_extrashort),
    condition = factor(condition, levels = c("Unadjusted", "Weighted", "Imputed")),
    var1_order = match(var1, rq6y),
    var2_order = ifelse(is.na(var2), 0, match(var2, rq6y))
  ) %>%
  arrange(param, condition, var1_order, var2_order, timepoint) %>%
  mutate(variable_label = factor(variable_label, levels = unique(variable_label))) %>%
  select(condition, timepoint, param, variable_label, y, ymin, ymax, pval) %>%
  group_by(condition, timepoint, param) %>%
  mutate(
    pval_adj = stats::p.adjust(pval, method = "holm")
  )

bias_summary %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  gt(groupname_col = c("param", "condition"), rowname_col = "variable_label") %>%
  cols_label(
    condition = "Condition",
    timepoint = "Timepoint",
    y = "Est",
    ymin = "LB",
    ymax = "UB",
    pval = md("p"),
    pval_adj = md("p<sub>Holm</sub>")
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(y, ymin, ymax),
    decimals = 3
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(pval, pval_adj),
    decimals = 4
  ) %>%
  # Styling - uniform font size
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(size = px(10)),
    locations = list(
      cells_body(),
      cells_stub(),
      cells_row_groups(),
      cells_column_labels()
    )
  ) %>%
  # Highlight significant positive (green)
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#ffd9d1"),
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = c(y, ymin, ymax, pval, pval_adj),
      rows = pval_adj < 0.05 & y > 0
    )
  ) %>%
  # Highlight significant negative (red)
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#b6c3e0"),
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = c(y, ymin, ymax, pval, pval_adj),
      rows = pval_adj < 0.05 & y < 0
    )
  ) %>%
  # Footnotes
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = md("<em>Note.</em> Est = Estimate, LB = Lower Bound 95% CI, UB = Upper Bound 95% CI. Significant (p<sub>adj</sub> < 0.05) effects highlighted in green (increases) or red (decreases). SMD = (Mean<sub>condition</sub> - Mean<sub>original</sub>) / SD<sub>original</sub>. Variance % change = (Var<sub>condition</sub> - Var<sub>original</sub>) / Var<sub>original</sub>. Correlation change = r<sub>condition</sub> - r<sub>original</sub>."),
    placement = "right"
  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = "P values are Bonferroni-Holm adjusted within each condition × timepoint × parameter group",
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = pval_adj),
    placement = "right"
  ) %>%
  opt_footnote_marks(marks = c("*", "†"))

Bias Reduction: IP Weighted vs Unadjusted Attritioned Estimates

These results test if the weighted attritioned estimates are significantly more or less biased than unadjusted attritioned estimates. For each outcome/parameter and timepoint, the table reports the proportional change in bias, (BiasUnadjusted − BiasWeighted) / BiasUnadjusted, the proportion of bootstrap iterations where weighting reduced bias (Pbetter), and a Holm-adjusted p-value; blue shading indicates weighting significantly reduced bias, red indicates it significantly increased bias.

Code
# Prepare diffratio1 table (Unadjusted - Weighted) / Unadjusted
diffratio1_summary = combined_results_wide %>%
  select(param, variable_raw, timepoint, pbetter1,
         y = diffratio1_y, ymin = diffratio1_ymin, ymax = diffratio1_ymax) %>%
  # Add variable labels
  mutate(
    var1 = case_when(
      param == "cor" ~ str_extract(variable_raw, "^[^_]+"),
      TRUE ~ variable_raw
    ),
    var2 = case_when(
      param == "cor" ~ str_extract(variable_raw, "[^_]+$"),
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    var1_label = rq6y_labels[match(var1, rq6y)],
    var2_label = rq6y_labels[match(var2, rq6y)],
    variable_label = case_when(
      param == "cor" ~ paste0(var1_label, " × ", var2_label),
      TRUE ~ var1_label
    ),
    param = case_when(
      param == "smd" ~ "Standardized Mean Difference",
      param == "var" ~ "Variance % Change",
      param == "cor" ~ "Correlation Change",
      TRUE ~ param
    ),
    param = factor(param, levels = c("Standardized Mean Difference", "Variance % Change", "Correlation Change")),
    timepoint = factor(timepoint, levels = rq1y_twin_labels_clean_extrashort),
    var1_order = match(var1, rq6y),
    var2_order = ifelse(is.na(var2), 0, match(var2, rq6y))
  ) %>%
  arrange(param, var1_order, var2_order, timepoint) %>%
  mutate(variable_label = factor(variable_label, levels = unique(variable_label))) %>%
  select(param, timepoint, variable_label, y, ymin, ymax, pbetter1) %>%
  mutate(p_val = bayestestR::pd_to_p(pmax(pbetter1, 1 - pbetter1))) %>%
  group_by(param, timepoint) %>%
  mutate(p_adj = p.adjust(p_val, method = "holm")) %>%
  ungroup()

diffratio1_summary %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  gt(groupname_col = "param", rowname_col = "variable_label") %>%
  cols_label(
    timepoint = "Timepoint",
    y = "Est",
    ymin = "LB",
    ymax = "UB",
    pbetter1 = md("P<sub>better</sub>"),
    p_val = md("p"),
    p_adj = md("p<sub>adj</sub>")
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(y, ymin, ymax, pbetter1), decimals = 3) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(p_val, p_adj), decimals = 3) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(size = px(10)),
    locations = list(
      cells_body(), cells_stub(), cells_row_groups(), cells_column_labels()
    )
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#b6c3e0"),
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = c(y, ymin, ymax, pbetter1, p_val, p_adj),
      rows = p_adj < 0.05 & pbetter1 > 0.5
    )
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#ffd9d1"),
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = c(y, ymin, ymax, pbetter1, p_val, p_adj),
      rows = p_adj < 0.05 & pbetter1 < 0.5
    )
  ) %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Bias Reduction: Weighting vs Unadjusted",
    subtitle = md("(Bias<sub>Unadjusted</sub> − Bias<sub>Weighted</sub>) / Bias<sub>Unadjusted</sub>")
  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = md("<em>Note.</em> Est = Estimate, LB = Lower Bound 95% CI, UB = Upper Bound 95% CI. Significant (p<sub>adj</sub> < 0.05) effects highlighted in blue (weighting reduces bias) or red (weighting increases bias)."),
    placement = "right"
  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = md("P<sub>better</sub> = proportion of bootstrap iterations where |Bias<sub>Weighted</sub>| < |Bias<sub>Unadjusted</sub>|. Values > 0.5 indicate weighting reduces bias; values < 0.5 indicate weighting increases bias."),
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = pbetter1),
    placement = "right"
  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = md("p = two-tailed p-value equivalent derived from P<sub>better</sub> using bayestestR::pd_to_p(). Computed as 2 × min(P<sub>better</sub>, 1 − P<sub>better</sub>)."),
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = p_val),
    placement = "right"
  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = "p_adj = Holm-corrected p-value within each parameter type × timepoint group.",
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = p_adj),
    placement = "right"
  ) %>%
  opt_footnote_marks(marks = c("*", "†", "‡", "§"))

Bias Reduction: Imputed vs Unadjusted Attritioned Estimates

These results test if the imputed attritioned estimates are significantly more or less biased than unadjusted attritioned estimates. As above, the table reports the proportional change in bias, (BiasUnadjusted − BiasImputed) / BiasUnadjusted, the proportion of bootstrap iterations where imputation reduced bias (Pbetter), and a Holm-adjusted p-value; blue shading indicates imputation significantly reduced bias, red indicates it significantly increased bias.

Code
# Prepare diffratio2 table (Unadjusted - Imputed) / Unadjusted
diffratio2_summary = combined_results_wide %>%
  select(param, variable_raw, timepoint, pbetter2,
         y = diffratio2_y, ymin = diffratio2_ymin, ymax = diffratio2_ymax) %>%

    var1 = case_when(
      param == "cor" ~ str_extract(variable_raw, "^[^_]+"),

      param == "cor" ~ str_extract(variable_raw, "[^_]+$"),
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    var1_label = rq6y_labels[match(var1, rq6y)],
    var2_label = rq6y_labels[match(var2, rq6y)],
    variable_label = case_when(
      param == "cor" ~ paste0(var1_label, " × ", var2_label),
      TRUE ~ var1_label
    ),
    param = case_when(
      param == "smd" ~ "Standardized Mean Difference",
      param == "var" ~ "Variance % Change",

    ),

    var2_order = ifelse(is.na(var2), 0, match(var2, rq6y))
  ) %>%

  mutate(variable_label = factor(variable_label, levels = unique(variable_label))) %>%

diffratio2_summary %>%

  fmt_number(columns = c(p_val, p_adj), decimals = 3) %>%

    )

    locations = cells_body(
      columns = c(y, ymin, ymax, pbetter2, p_val, p_adj),

    )
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#ffd9d1"),
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = c(y, ymin, ymax, pbetter2, p_val, p_adj),
      rows = p_adj < 0.05 & pbetter2 < 0.5
    )
  ) %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Bias Reduction: Imputed vs Unadjusted",
    subtitle = md("(Bias<sub>Unadjusted</sub> − Bias<sub>Imputed</sub>) / Bias<sub>Unadjusted</sub>")
  ) %>%

    footnote = md("<em>Note.</em> Est = Estimate, LB = Lower Bound 95% CI, UB = Upper Bound 95% CI. Significant (p<sub>adj</sub> < 0.05) effects highlighted in blue (imputation reduces bias) or red (imputation increases bias)."),
    placement = "right"
  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = md("P<sub>better</sub> = proportion of bootstrap iterations where |Bias<sub>Imputed</sub>| < |Bias<sub>Unadjusted</sub>|. Values > 0.5 indicate imputation reduces bias; values < 0.5 indicate imputation increases bias."),
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = pbetter2),
    placement = "right"
  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = md("p = two-tailed p-value equivalent derived from P<sub>better</sub> using bayestestR::pd_to_p(). Computed as 2 × min(P<sub>better</sub>, 1 − P<sub>better</sub>)."),
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = p_val),
    placement = "right"
  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = "p_adj = Holm-corrected p-value within each parameter type × timepoint group.",
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = p_adj),
    placement = "right"
  ) %>%
  opt_footnote_marks(marks = c("*", "†", "‡", "§"))

ACE Estimates

RQ3: Comparison of Unadjusted/Weighted/Imputed Attritioned Estimates to Original Estimates

The table below compares the ACE (Additive genetic, shared environment, non-shared environment) variance component estimates from the Unadjusted, IP-Weighted, and Imputed attritioned samples to the original full-sample estimates, separately by sex, outcome, and attrition timepoint. It reports the difference (attritioned condition − original) with 95% CIs and Bonferroni-Holm adjusted p-values (adjusted within each condition × timepoint × sex group); significant increases are shaded orange and decreases blue.

Code
ace_diff_combined = bind_rows(ace_diff_unadj, ace_diff_weigh, ace_diff_imput) %>%
  mutate(
    condition = factor(condition, levels = c("Unadjusted", "Weighted", "Imputed")),
    timepoint = factor(timepoint, levels = rq1y_twin_labels_clean_extrashort),
    par       = toupper(par),
    sex       = str_to_title(sex)
  ) %>%
  group_by(condition, timepoint, sex) %>%
  mutate(pval_adj = stats::p.adjust(pval, method = "holm")) %>%
  ungroup()

ace_diff_combined %>%
  select(sex, condition, timepoint, par, name_clean, y, ymin, ymax, pval, pval_adj) %>%
  arrange(sex, name_clean, par, condition, timepoint) %>%
  gt(groupname_col = "sex") %>%
  cols_label(
    condition  = "Condition",
    timepoint  = "Timepoint",
    par        = "Par",
    name_clean = "Variable",
    y          = "Est",
    ymin       = "Lower",
    ymax       = "Upper",
    pval       = md("p"),
    pval_adj   = md("p<sub>adj</sub>")
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(y, ymin, ymax), decimals = 3) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(pval, pval_adj), decimals = 4) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(size = px(10)),
    locations = list(
      cells_body(), cells_stub(), cells_row_groups(), cells_column_labels()
    )
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#ffd9d1"),
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = c(y, ymin, ymax, pval, pval_adj),
      rows = pval_adj < 0.05 & y > 0
    )
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#b6c3e0"),
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = c(y, ymin, ymax, pval, pval_adj),
      rows = pval_adj < 0.05 & y < 0
    )
  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = md("<em>Note.</em> Difference = Attritioned − Original. Par: A = additive genetic, C = shared environment, E = unique environment. Significant (p<sub>adj</sub> < 0.05) effects highlighted in orange (increases) or blue (decreases). P values Bonferroni-Holm adjusted within each condition × timepoint × sex group."),
    placement = "right"
  )

Discussion

Relationship between maternal education and child outcomes

In some analyses, maternal education is treated as a numeric variable (1-8), which assumes a linear relationship with child outcomes. To check whether this assumption is reasonable, we examine the predicted child education & cognition outcomes at each maternal education level.

We regress child outcomes on maternal education using dummy coding (i.e., treating each education level as a separate category). The plots below show the predicted outcome for each education level. If the linearity assumption holds, these points should fall approximately on a straight line.

We find that mothers with A Levels have generally similar child outcomes to those with Higher National Certificate and Higher National Diploma qualifications. Thus, the assumption of linearity seems unreasonable, and it might be problematic to have these two categories as separate numeric codes.

Code
# Helper function to create marginal effects plot
plot_education_effects = function(model, y_label) {
  marginaleffects::predictions(model, by = "amohqual") %>%
    data.frame() %>%
    rename(
      prediction = estimate,
      education_level = amohqual
    ) %>%
    ggplot(aes(y = prediction, x = education_level, group = 1)) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), width = 0.2) +
    geom_point(size = 2) +
    geom_line() +
    labs(
      x = "Maternal Education Level",
      y = y_label
    ) +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(
      axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1)
    )
}

Distribution of maternal education: full sample vs. Y26 Webtest participants

The plot below compares the distribution of maternal education (amohqual) between the full TEDS sample and those who participated at the Y26 Webtest (zcdata1 == 1). Bars show the proportion of mothers at each education level within each group.

Code
df %>%
  # filter(twin==1) %>% 
  select(zcdata1, amohqual) %>%
  mutate(fullsample = 1) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(fullsample, zcdata1), names_to = "group", values_to = "participated") %>%
  filter(participated == 1, !is.na(amohqual)) %>%
  mutate(group = if_else(group == "fullsample", "Full sample", "Y26 Webtest participants")) %>%
  group_by(group, amohqual) %>%
  summarise(n = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(amohqual = factor(amohqual, levels = levels(df$amohqual))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = amohqual, y = prop, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = scales::percent(prop, accuracy = 0.1)),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.9),
    vjust = -0.4,
    size = 2.5
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Full sample" = "#d53031", "Y26 Webtest participants" = "#00929c")) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "inside",
    legend.position.inside = c(0.98, 0.98),
    legend.justification = c("right", "top"),
    legend.background = element_rect(colour = "grey80")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Maternal Education Level",
    y = "Proportion",
    fill = "Group"
  )
